Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, this new design offers improved sensitivity at high frequencies or better signal-to-noise ratios for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms, offering promising possibilities for future gravitational wave detectors.

This study provides a detailed examination of the potential inaccuracies in
the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced ensemble method that surpasses
earlier contextualized approaches and apply it to investigate the levels of
semantic change in English vocabulary over the course of 5 decades. Our
results show that contextualized methods may inaccurately predict significant
change in words with little to no actual semantic evolution, or whose
status remains unclear. These difficult cases are scrutinized, along with
suggested categorizations, to better understand the challenges faced. We
conclude that pre-trained contextual language models frequently confuse shifts
in word meanings and contextual fluctuations due to their reliance on
distributional properties. Moreover, they often blend the grammatical and
semantics components of words, differing from issues seen with static

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. Our primary focus is on the size of this set for various types of graphs and networks that are commonly studied in mathematics and computer science. We examine how beta_k varies in different graph topologies, investigate its relationship with other similar graphical properties, and look into identifying sets of size 2 in various specific graph types. Additionally, we conduct an exhaustive analysis of beta_k in discrete cubes, specifically in hyper-cubes of varying dimensions, and derive precise figures for beta_k in many cases. In particular, we find that beta_k in an n-dimensional hyper-cube is 1 if n is 1, 2 if n is greater than 2, and co-relates beta_k with beta_k~ in the binary tensor product of graphs. To determine beta_k in general network topology, we also outline an efficient algorithm that can pinpoint each vertex in a graph by determining their distance to every point in an identifying set, and use this algorithm as a component in determining beta_k. Lastly, we explore a more intuitive alternative for defining beta_k and its equivalent variation and conclude that they are identical in definition. -Abstract.

Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques. Moreover, possible sizes for non-binary GCM quadruples are defined as unlimited in theory but are only verified for specific instances. An example construction for a quaternary GCA quad in a four-dimensional space is provided. Theoretical groundwork also involves deriving properties of GCA components, particularly identity-preserving transformations and bijective mappings. Lastly, various types of GCA subarrays are shown to possess Golay complementary properties, enabling the utilization of existing GC matrices as GCA components. A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining this area through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this area, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Segmentation (PBLS) consisting of multiple stages to define the treated brain area in images taken before and after LITT through a combination of artificial intelligence models and data manipulation. Furthermore, to reduce the need for a large initial data set, the authors suggest a novel structure called Bi-Task Variational Auto-Encoder (BTVAE) to define the treated area in the initial images taken before LITT. The results of the BTVAE model on a small data set were highly precise and comparable to the precision achieved on a larger data set, demonstrating its effectiveness and potential applications in various medical treatments. The code and data sets used in this research are available for other scientists to review and utilize.

The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. Furthermore, our code and pre-trained models are available for public use, providing a foundation for future research on structured knowledge utilization by large language models.

While initial studies on VSI took into account a simple model of a disk with little to no particle influence, new research suggests that dust particle growth might actually counteract VSI. Anoretical model predicting VSI damping could also delay its onset, modelers are advised. To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. The design of the MuLE optics can be easily scaled up or down based on the size of the available image sensor.
